explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The serpent asks, “Did God really say, ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden?’…” but that's his question, not her answer. The woman answers, “We may eat the fruit of the trees of the garden…” and then she points to one tree in the middle. Her answer has a whole lot more yes in it than his question did.

That's right. The woman answers the serpent, “We may eat the fruit of the trees of the garden…” Only the tree in the middle of the garden is the exception. She read the whole sign, baker, not just the first word. The serpent's question made it sound like a whole lot of NO, and she didn't let it stand.

Yes, baker. The woman tells the serpent that God has said, “You must not eat of it or touch it, or you will die.” Notice she even adds “…or touch it…” She's repeating the warning, and she's not shrinking it down to something small. Then the serpent answers with, “You will not surely die…” Those two lines are going head to head.

Close to a nap, but no. The woman never says anything about sleep. She says God has said, “You must not eat of it or touch it, or you will die.” It's a much heavier word than sleep, and she says it plainly.

Sick is a step short of what she says. The woman tells the serpent that God has said, “You must not eat of it or touch it, or you will die.” She doesn't mention a stomachache or a fever. The word she uses is die, and it's the heaviest one in the whole conversation.

That's it. The serpent tells her, “You will not surely die…” She has just told him that God said they would die, and his answer is a flat contradiction. No warm-up and no hedging, just a smooth NO. Then he keeps talking, this time about what God knows (Genesis 3:5).

That line sounds like something a sneaky person would say, but the serpent never says it. What he says is, “You will not surely die…” He goes straight at what God said about dying. Nothing in the text has him talking about God finding out.

explanations.answer: God will not mind at all
explanations.explanation: Nope, the serpent doesn't say that. He tells the woman, “You will not surely die…” Then he starts talking about what God knows (Genesis 3:5). But he never says a word about God not minding.
Yes. The serpent says, “…you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” Not like angels, not like kings. Like God. That's not a small offer, friend, and it comes straight from the serpent's mouth.

Angels would be a big promise, but it's not the one the serpent makes. He says, “…you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” The serpent skips right past angels and goes straight to the top. That's quite a reach.

Kings would sound pretty fancy, friend, but the serpent aims higher than that. He says they will be “…like God, knowing good and evil.” No crowns and no thrones come up in what he says. He goes right to God.

explanations.answer: She takes the fruit and eats it
explanations.explanation: Yes. The text says it plainly: “…she took the fruit and ate it.” I think this is one of the quietest, heaviest moments in the whole Bible. There's no big drum roll in the text. She takes, and she eats.

explanations.answer: She walks away from the tree
explanations.explanation: I wish the story went that way, but the text says something else. She doesn't walk away. She “…took the fruit and ate it.” This is where the whole story turns, and it's a heavy moment.

explanations.answer: She asks the serpent to leave
explanations.explanation: That would've been a different story, baker. The text never has her send the serpent away. Instead, she “…took the fruit and ate it.” That's the heavy turning point.
The text says otherwise. She gave some to “…her husband who was with her…” He wasn't off somewhere else in the garden. He was right there at her side when it happened.
That's right. The text says she gave some “…to her husband who was with her, and he ate it.” He wasn't wandering off to check on the garden. He was standing right there beside her.

Yes. The text says “…they sewed together fig leaves and made coverings for themselves.” Sewing leaves together, friend. That's real craftwork. My mustache can pack a cookie box all day, but I wouldn't trust it with a sewing job.

Palm branches sound sturdy, but that's not what's in the text. It says “…they sewed together fig leaves and made coverings for themselves.” Fig leaves are what they used. Palm branches don't come up in this story.

Reeds would be a creative choice, baker, but the text doesn't mention them. It says “…they sewed together fig leaves and made coverings for themselves.” Fig leaves are what they sewed. No river reeds anywhere.

Yes. The text says they “…hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden.” First they heard His voice walking in the garden, and then they went in among the trees. I think that's a heavy kind of hiding. The text says it plainly.

The text says they did. When they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden, they “…hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden.” They didn't come running out to meet Him. They went the other way, into the trees.

explanations.answer: He was afraid because he was naked
explanations.explanation: Yes. The man says, “I heard Your voice in the garden, and I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself.” That's his own answer, in his own words. Notice he gives it straight when God calls out to him.

explanations.answer: He was ashamed of what the serpent said
explanations.explanation: The man never brings up the serpent here. His answer is, “I heard Your voice in the garden, and I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself.” He says afraid, and he says naked. Those are the two things he names.

explanations.answer: He was busy working in the garden
explanations.explanation: Working in the garden is a fair guess, friend. But the man's answer is, “I heard Your voice in the garden, and I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself.” He says nothing about work. He says he was afraid, and he says he was naked. That's the reason he gives for hiding.

Close, but the serpent isn't who the man names. He says, “The woman whom You gave me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.” The serpent doesn't even come up in his answer. The woman is the one he points to.

That's right. The man answers, “The woman whom You gave me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.” He talks about the woman, not the serpent. The serpent doesn't show up in his answer at all.

That's it. She answers, “The serpent deceived me…” and then adds, “…and I ate…” The LORD God asked her one short question, and she gave one short answer. She names the serpent as the one who deceived her.
The man was right there with her, but she doesn't name him. She says, “The serpent deceived me…” and then, “…and I ate…” The word deceived goes with the serpent in her answer.
She doesn't blame the tree, friend. Her answer is, “The serpent deceived me…” and then, “…and I ate…” The serpent is the one she names. The tree stays out of it.

explanations.answer: Her seed will crush the serpent's head
explanations.explanation: Yes. The LORD God says to the serpent, “He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.” The head that gets crushed is the serpent's, since God is speaking to the serpent. The one doing the crushing comes from the woman's side of that line. The serpent's part in the verse is the strike to the heel.

explanations.answer: The serpent will crush her seed's head
explanations.explanation: That one is flipped around, baker. The LORD God tells the serpent, “He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.” The head that gets crushed is the serpent's. What the serpent gets to strike is a heel.

explanations.answer: The serpent's seed will crush her head
explanations.explanation: Close, but it's turned around. The LORD God says to the serpent, “He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.” Your head is the serpent's head, because God is speaking to the serpent. The strike to the heel is what the serpent does. Read those pronouns slowly, baker, and the picture comes clear.

Yes. The LORD God says to the woman, “Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.” It comes right after what He says about pain in childbirth. It's a heavy part of what He tells her.

The text says He does. After speaking about pain in childbirth, the LORD God tells the woman, “Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.” It's part of what He says to her in this moment, and it's a heavy part.
That's right. The LORD God says, “through toil you will eat of it all the days of your life.” Toil. Even the word sounds tired. That's what the ground will take from him from now on.

Trading is a smart idea, friend, but it's not in the text. The LORD God says, “through toil you will eat of it all the days of your life.” The food comes from the ground, and the work is toil. No market stalls in this verse.

The text doesn't send him out hunting. The LORD God says, “through toil you will eat of it all the days of your life.” He adds, “…you will eat the plants of the field.” So it's toil and plants, not a chase.

Yes. The LORD God says Adam will return to the ground “…because out of it were you taken.” Then He says, “For dust you are, and to dust you shall return.” Dust is the word He uses for what Adam is. It's a heavy line, and the text just says it plainly.

Breath does show up at the start of the man's story. God “breathed the breath of life into his nostrils” (Genesis 2:7). But here the LORD God says, “For dust you are, and to dust you shall return.” The word He uses is dust.
Water is a good guess, baker, but the text goes another way. The LORD God says, “For dust you are, and to dust you shall return.” Dust is the word. It's heavy, and it's what the man was taken from.

explanations.answer: She would be the mother of all the living
explanations.explanation: Yes. The text says Adam named his wife Eve “…because she would be the mother of all the living.” The man is Adam, and his wife is Eve. It's the reason the text gives, so it's the one I'll go with.

explanations.answer: She would watch over the whole garden
explanations.explanation: That's a big job, but the text doesn't give it to her. It says Adam named his wife Eve “…because she would be the mother of all the living.” That's the whole reason, straight from the text.

explanations.answer: She would help him work the ground
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give that as the reason. Adam named his wife Eve “…because she would be the mother of all the living.” That's her name, and that's why he gave it to her.

That's right. The text says, “…the LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them.” Earlier they had sewn fig leaves together for themselves. Now the garments come from Him.
The text says He does. “…the LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them.” Earlier they had sewn fig leaves together for themselves. Now the garments come from Him.

Not this time, friend. The text says, “Therefore the LORD God banished him from the Garden of Eden to work the ground from which he had been taken.” He doesn't get to stay. He's sent out, and it's a heavy moment.

That's right, baker. The man doesn't stay in the garden. The text says the LORD God “…banished him from the Garden of Eden to work the ground from which he had been taken.” Right before that, the LORD God speaks of the man reaching out to take from the tree of life and living forever (Genesis 3:22). I think this is one of the heavy parts of the story.

explanations.answer: Cherubim and a whirling sword of flame
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! The text says He “…stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden, along with a whirling sword of flame to guard the way to the tree of life.” Cherubim AND a sword of flame that whirls. I think the way back looks closed here, and that part is heavy. But the story isn't over.

That's a fiery pair, baker, but it's not what's in this verse. The text says He “…stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden, along with a whirling sword of flame…” Cherubim, and a sword. No burning coal.

explanations.answer: A pillar of fire and cloud
explanations.explanation: That's a fiery guess, but it's not in this verse. The text says He “…stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden, along with a whirling sword of flame to guard the way to the tree of life.” The guards here are cherubim and a sword. No pillar and no cloud.
That's it. The text says He “…stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden…” East is where they stand, along with the whirling sword of flame. You read your compass well, friend.
West is a fair guess, but the compass points the other way. The text says He “…stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden…” East is where the cherubim stand.

North sounds sensible, baker, but the text says something else. He “…stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden…” The guards stand on the east side, along with the whirling sword of flame. So turn that compass a quarter turn. North can sit this one out.
